CONCURRENT_REQUESTS.summary: CONCURRENT_REQUESTS sets Scrapy’s global limit for simultaneous downloader requests. For broad crawls, the documentation suggests starting at 100 and tuning it based on CPU and memory use.
CONCURRENT_REQUESTS.explanation: CONCURRENT_REQUESTS sets the global limit for downloader requests that run at the same time. Raising it can help a broad crawl process many domains in parallel, but it also increases memory use. Choose a value by testing CPU and memory use.

parameters.name: CONCURRENT_REQUESTS
parameters.description: Maximum number of simultaneous requests performed by the downloader. Use 0 for no limit.

CONCURRENT_REQUESTS.returns: A settings value that controls the global downloader concurrency limit.

example.title: Raise global concurrency
example.code: CONCURRENT_REQUESTS = 100
example.explanation: Set this in settings.py to allow up to 100 downloader requests at the same time.

useCases.title: Process many domains in parallel
useCases.scenario: Many-domain crawl

useCases.title: Increase throughput after testing CPU and memory limits
useCases.scenario: Performance tuning

interview.question: What does CONCURRENT_REQUESTS control?
interview.answer: CONCURRENT_REQUESTS is the global maximum number of downloader requests that can run at the same time. The default is 16.
interview.followUp: How would you tune it? Test several values and choose one where CPU use is about 80–90%, while checking memory use.

interview.question: How is the global limit different from the per-domain limit?
interview.answer: It limits requests across the whole Scrapy downloader, not only requests to one domain. A separate per-domain limit is controlled by CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN.
interview.followUp: What should you change for a broad crawl? Raise the global limit and review the per-domain limit so it does not become the bottleneck.

interview.question: How should you choose a value for a broad crawl?
interview.answer: A value of 100 is a useful starting point for a broad crawl. The suitable value depends on the CPU and memory available to the crawler.
interview.followUp: What other resource can slow high-concurrency crawls? DNS resolution can become slow because Scrapy uses a blocking resolver thread pool.

keyPoints: The setting limits simultaneous downloader requests across the crawler.
Set it to 0 to remove the global request limit.
For a broad crawl, 100 is suggested as a starting value.
Use testing to find a value that keeps CPU use near 80–90%.
gotchas: A higher value can use more memory. Lower the limit if memory becomes a problem.
The default is aimed at focused crawls, not many-domain crawls. Broad crawls usually need a higher value.

CrawlerProcess.summary: CrawlerProcess runs Scrapy from a Python script. It starts the reactor, schedules spiders with crawl(), and runs them with start().
CrawlerProcess.explanation: CrawlerProcess starts and manages the reactor for a script. Call crawl() to schedule a spider, then start() to run it until the crawl finishes. Use CrawlerRunner instead when the application already manages the reactor.

parameters.name: settings
parameters.description: Optional Scrapy settings used by the crawler process or runner.

parameters.name: crawl spider
parameters.description: Spider class or spider name, plus spider arguments.

parameters.name: spider arguments
parameters.description: Arguments passed to the spider when it is created.

CrawlerProcess.returns: crawl() returns an awaitable task; start() runs until scheduled crawling finishes.

example.title: Run a spider from a Python script
example.explanation: This creates a crawler process, starts one spider, and writes items to a JSON file.

useCases.title: Standalone scripts
useCases.scenario: A Python script needs to run one or more spiders and finish after crawling.

useCases.title: Scrapy project scripts
useCases.scenario: A project wants to reuse its configured settings and locate a spider by name.

useCases.title: Existing asyncio applications
useCases.scenario: A notebook or ASGI application already owns an asyncio event loop.

interview.question: When should you use AsyncCrawlerProcess?
interview.answer: AsyncCrawlerProcess is the simple choice for a standalone script. It starts the reactor, configures logging, and stops after the scheduled crawl finishes.
interview.followUp: What should an application use if it already owns the reactor? Use AsyncCrawlerRunner and run the spider in that existing reactor.

interview.question: How do you run multiple spiders in one process?
interview.answer: Call crawl() for each spider and then call start(). The process blocks until all scheduled crawling jobs finish.
interview.followUp: How can two spiders run at the same time? Schedule both with crawl() before calling start().

interview.question: How can Scrapy use an existing asyncio loop?
interview.answer: Use AsyncCrawlerRunner with TWISTED_REACTOR_ENABLED set to False when an existing asyncio event loop should run Scrapy. This is useful for environments such as notebook kernels or ASGI applications.
interview.followUp: What is a limitation of this mode? The documentation calls running without a Twisted reactor experimental and points to additional limitations.

keyPoints: AsyncCrawlerProcess is the main helper for running a spider from a standalone script.
The process helper starts the Twisted reactor and prepares logging and shutdown handling.
Pass a settings dictionary when creating the crawler process.
With AsyncCrawlerRunner, handle crawl errors where the returned task is awaited.
Choose AsyncCrawlerRunner when another part of the application already runs the Twisted reactor.
AsyncCrawlerRunner.join() waits until all currently scheduled crawler tasks finish.
gotchas: A script needs a Twisted reactor or an asyncio event loop. The process helper can start the required runtime.
Multiple spiders do not share crawler objects, middleware instances, or resolved settings.
The no-reactor mode may have limitations. Use it carefully, especially in production applications.

CrawlSpider.summary: CrawlSpider is a Spider subclass for regular websites that follows links according to ordered Rule objects. Subclass it, define standard spider attributes, and use rules to describe link selection and callbacks.
CrawlSpider.explanation: CrawlSpider is a Spider subclass for crawling regular websites through declarative Rule objects. It extracts links, selects the first matching rule in declaration order, creates requests using that rule, and processes the resulting responses with the rule callback; start responses are handled through parse_start_url.

example.title: CrawlSpider with an ordered link rule
example.explanation: A CrawlSpider applies its ordered rules to links extracted from responses, sending matching links to the configured callback. Subclass it, define the usual spider attributes, and provide rules describing link-following behavior.

useCases.title: Rule-based site traversal
useCases.scenario: A site has predictable internal URL patterns and pages should be crawled automatically.

useCases.title: Pattern-specific parsing
useCases.scenario: Several link patterns need different callbacks or extraction behavior.

useCases.title: Reusable crawling scaffold
useCases.scenario: A project needs a reusable generic crawler starting from one or more URLs.

interview.question: What problem does CrawlSpider solve?
interview.answer: CrawlSpider is a Spider subclass designed for regular websites. Its rules describe link-following behavior, so the crawler can generate requests without manually implementing every link traversal.
interview.followUp: How does it choose among overlapping rules? It uses the first matching rule according to the order in the rules attribute.

interview.question: What is the purpose of rules?
interview.answer: The rules attribute is a sequence of Rule objects. Each Rule defines a particular crawling behavior, such as which links to select and how to process their responses.
interview.followUp: What should be changed for highly custom traversal? Override the relevant behavior or implement a regular Spider when the generic rule model is not suitable.

interview.question: How are start responses handled?
interview.answer: parse_start_url handles responses from start_urls and can parse initial content before rule-driven crawling continues. Its result must be an item, a request, or an iterable containing those types.
interview.followUp: How can a spider customize processing after a rule callback? Use the rule's callback and the CrawlSpider response-processing hooks rather than relying on the default parser alone.

keyPoints: Use CrawlSpider as a convenient starting point for ordinary website crawling.
Link traversal is declared through rules instead of being fully hand-coded.
The class retains the standard Spider attributes, which the subclass must define as appropriate.
gotchas: Rule order matters: when several rules match a link, only the first matching rule is selected.

DOWNLOAD_DELAY.summary: Scrapy settings configure components and request downloading. Use global settings for defaults and DOWNLOAD_SLOTS for per-domain concurrency, delays, and jitter.
DOWNLOAD_DELAY.explanation: Scrapy settings are key-value options used by the engine, extensions, pipelines, and spiders. You select a settings module with SCRAPY_SETTINGS_MODULE, then values are combined from several sources; command-line values have the highest priority. Download settings control request timing, timeouts, response sizes, and per-domain limits.

parameters.description: Python import path of the settings module, such as myproject.settings.

parameters.name: DOWNLOAD_DELAY
parameters.description: Minimum seconds between consecutive requests to the same domain.

parameters.name: DOWNLOAD_DELAY_JITTER
parameters.description: Random variation applied to DOWNLOAD_DELAY; zero disables it.

parameters.name: DOWNLOAD_BIND_ADDRESS
parameters.description: Local outgoing host, or a host-and-port tuple.

parameters.name: DOWNLOAD_SLOTS
parameters.description: Per-slot concurrency, delay, and jitter mapping.

parameters.name: DOWNLOAD_TIMEOUT
parameters.description: Downloader timeout in seconds.

parameters.name: DOWNLOAD_MAXSIZE
parameters.description: Maximum response body size in bytes; zero disables the limit.

parameters.name: DOWNLOAD_WARNSIZE
parameters.description: Response size at which Scrapy logs a warning; zero disables the warning.

example.explanation: This sets a global delay and disables its random variation. Requests for example.com use their own slot settings.

useCases.title: Throttle crawling
useCases.scenario: Slow down requests to reduce load on a website.

useCases.title: Per-domain control
useCases.scenario: Apply different limits to different domains.

useCases.title: Limit response size
useCases.scenario: Prevent very large responses from consuming resources.

useCases.title: Bind download connections
useCases.scenario: Use a specific local interface for outgoing connections.

interview.question: What do DOWNLOAD_DELAY and DOWNLOAD_DELAY_JITTER control?
interview.answer: DOWNLOAD_DELAY sets the minimum wait between two requests to the same domain. DOWNLOAD_DELAY_JITTER adds random variation around that delay; a value of zero disables the variation.
interview.followUp: How would you configure different limits for two domains? Use DOWNLOAD_SLOTS with a mapping for each domain, including delay, concurrency, and jitter values.

interview.question: How does per-domain throttling work?
interview.answer: DOWNLOAD_SLOTS configures concurrency and timing per download slot, usually one slot per URL domain. For fields not given in a slot, Scrapy uses DOWNLOAD_DELAY, CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN, and DOWNLOAD_DELAY_JITTER.
interview.followUp: How can a request use a slot that is not its URL domain? Set Request.meta['download_slot'] to the desired slot name; redirects keep that slot name.

interview.question: What does DOWNLOAD_MAXSIZE do?
interview.answer: DOWNLOAD_MAXSIZE limits the response body in bytes, both before and after compression. A value of zero disables the limit, and a larger response is aborted and ignored.
interview.followUp: Can one request use a different limit? Yes. Set the download_maxsize Request.meta key for that request.

keyPoints: Set SCRAPY_SETTINGS_MODULE to a Python import path such as myproject.settings, and make sure Python can import that module.
Settings can come from several levels. Command-line values override spider values, which override project values.
DOWNLOAD_DELAY controls the minimum interval between consecutive requests to one domain. Decimal values are allowed.
DOWNLOAD_DELAY_JITTER controls random variation around DOWNLOAD_DELAY. For example, 0.2 varies the delay from 80% to 120%.
DOWNLOAD_BIND_ADDRESS chooses the local address for download connections. It can be a host string or a host-and-port tuple.
DOWNLOAD_TIMEOUT sets the downloader timeout in seconds. Its documented default is 180.
DOWNLOAD_MAXSIZE limits response bodies to 1 GiB by default. It applies before and after decompression.
DOWNLOAD_WARNSIZE logs a warning when a response exceeds the configured size. Set it to zero to disable this warning.
gotchas: A delay can reduce the real concurrency for a domain. If responses arrive faster than the delay, that domain may effectively use only one request at a time.
Per-slot settings normally use the URL domain. A custom download_slot value in Request.meta can assign a request to another slot.
A request can override the global timeout through its download_timeout metadata key.
Third-party download handlers might not support timeout or response-size checks.

Downloader middleware.summary: Downloader middleware provides hooks for changing Scrapy requests and responses at the HTTP level. Middleware order controls request and response processing, and hooks can continue, replace, reschedule, or handle work.
Downloader middleware.explanation: Downloader middleware adds hooks around Scrapy's HTTP request and response flow. Scrapy runs process_request methods in order, then runs process_response methods in reverse order. A middleware can continue processing, return a response, replace the request, or handle an exception.
Downloader middleware.syntax:
class DownloaderMiddleware:
    def process_request(self, request): ...
    def process_response(self, request, response): ...
    def process_exception(self, request, exception): ...

parameters.name: request
parameters.description: The request being processed or the request that caused the response or exception.

parameters.name: response
parameters.description: The response being processed by process_response.

parameters.name: exception
parameters.description: The exception raised during downloading or request processing.

Downloader middleware.returns: process_request: None, Response, Request, or IgnoreRequest. process_response: Response, Request, or IgnoreRequest. process_exception: None, Response, or Request.

example.explanation: This enables a custom middleware and disables the built-in user-agent middleware.

useCases.title: Customize outgoing requests
useCases.scenario: Add or change headers before a request is downloaded.

useCases.title: Control downloads

useCases.title: Download supporting data

interview.question: In what order do downloader middleware methods run?
interview.answer: Scrapy calls process_request for each middleware in increasing order. It calls process_response in decreasing order. This makes the first middleware closer to the engine and the last one closer to the downloader.
interview.followUp: What happens if process_request returns a Response? Scrapy skips the remaining process_request and process_exception methods and sends that response through process_response.

interview.question: What can process_request return?
interview.answer: process_request may return None, a Response, or a Request, or raise IgnoreRequest. None continues the normal chain; a Response stops downloading; and a returned Request is scheduled instead.
interview.followUp: What happens if process_response returns a Request? The response chain stops and Scrapy schedules that request for a later download.

interview.question: How can middleware handle download errors?
interview.answer: process_exception runs when a download handler or process_request raises an exception. Returning None passes the exception to the next middleware; returning a Response starts response processing; returning a Request reschedules work.
interview.followUp: What if no middleware handles the exception? Scrapy uses its default exception handling, including the request errback where applicable.

keyPoints: Enable a middleware by adding its class path and numeric order to DOWNLOADER_MIDDLEWARES.
Request hooks run from the lowest order to the highest order.
Response hooks run from the highest order back to the lowest order.
A Response from process_request prevents later request and exception hooks from running.
A returned Request stops the current request chain and schedules the new request.
Returning None from process_exception lets later exception handlers try to handle the error.
gotchas: Choose the order carefully because middleware can depend on work done by another middleware.
A middleware request must not wait for the request that is waiting for it.
When several requests need the same data, cache the download task to avoid starting duplicate downloads.

Field.summary: scrapy.Field is a dictionary-like metadata container used to declare fields on Scrapy Item subclasses. It can store configuration such as a serializer, while Scrapy records declared fields in Item.fields.
Field.explanation: Field is a metadata container used when declaring Scrapy item attributes. It behaves like a plain dictionary, so metadata can be supplied as keyword arguments; the declared Field objects are collected in the item’s fields mapping rather than remaining as class attributes.

parameters.name: **kwargs
parameters.description: Optional field metadata supplied as dictionary entries, commonly through keyword arguments such as serializer.

Field.returns: A plain dictionary containing the supplied field metadata.

example.title: Declare fields on an item
example.code:
import scrapy

class Product(scrapy.Item):
    name = scrapy.Field()
    price = scrapy.Field(serializer=float)

product = Product(name="Book", price="12.50")
assert product["price"] == "12.50"
assert product.fields["name"] == {}
example.explanation: Declare item fields with Field and optionally place metadata such as a serializer in the field mapping.

useCases.title: Declare item fields
useCases.scenario: Define the schema of scraped records with named attributes.

useCases.title: Store field metadata
useCases.scenario: Attach serializer or other processing metadata to a field.

useCases.title: Examine Item.fields

interview.question: What is scrapy.Field?
interview.answer: Field is used to declare an item field and hold metadata for it. The class itself is a plain dictionary alias, without extra functionality or attributes.
interview.followUp: Where can declaration metadata be inspected after class creation? In the Item.fields mapping, whose values are the Field objects used in the declaration.

interview.question: How can Field carry field metadata?
interview.answer: A Field can be created without metadata or with metadata entries such as serializer=str. Those entries provide a central place to describe how the field is handled internally.
interview.followUp: Does Field itself run the serializer? No; it stores metadata, while other Scrapy processing uses that metadata.

interview.question: How is Field used in an Item declaration?
interview.answer: Fields are declared as class attributes on an Item subclass, for example name = scrapy.Field(). Scrapy processes those declarations and stores them in the item’s fields attribute.
interview.followUp: What does the fields mapping contain? All declared fields, including fields that have not yet been populated.

keyPoints: Use Field declarations to keep per-field metadata alongside the item schema.
A field declaration centralizes metadata instead of scattering it across crawler components.
Item subclasses declare fields as class attributes, and Scrapy collects those declarations.
The Item schema rejects unknown field names, helping catch misspellings.
Item.fields maps each declared name to its corresponding Field metadata dictionary.
gotchas: Field is not a specialized field-value object: it is simply a dictionary alias and adds no behavior of its own.
Do not expect the declaration attribute to contain the Field after item construction; inspect the item’s fields mapping instead.

Item.summary: `scrapy.Item` is a dictionary-like container for structured data extracted by spiders. Define its permitted fields with `scrapy.Field()` and populate instances using normal mapping operations.
Item.explanation: Subclass `scrapy.Item` to define the fields a spider may produce. Each field is declared with `scrapy.Field()`, while the resulting object behaves like a dictionary for storing and accessing values; its `fields` mapping retains declarations and metadata.

parameters.name: args
parameters.description: Optional positional mapping or iterable accepted by the dictionary-like initializer.

parameters.name: kwargs

Item.returns: A new Item instance initialized from the supplied arguments.

example.title: Declare and populate an Item
example.code:
import scrapy

class Product(scrapy.Item):
    name = scrapy.Field()
    price = scrapy.Field()

product = Product(name="Book", price="12.99")
print(product["name"])
print(product.fields.keys())
example.explanation: Declares fields on a custom item, initializes values with keyword arguments, reads a value using dictionary syntax, and inspects all declared fields.

interview.question: What is `scrapy.Item`, and how do you define one?
interview.answer: `Item` is Scrapy's feature-complete item type with a dictionary-like API. A custom item subclasses `scrapy.Item` and declares its allowed fields with `Field` attributes.
interview.followUp: How does Scrapy recognize an item for pipelines? The documentation says `Item` is supported by itemadapter, so spider callback results of this type can be passed to item pipelines.

interview.question: How are values and field declarations accessed?
interview.answer: The class declaration creates the permitted field names, and instances store values using the standard dictionary interface. The declaration metadata is available through the instance's `fields` attribute.
interview.followUp: What does `fields` contain? It contains the declared field definitions, including fields that have not yet received values.

interview.question: Why use `Item` instead of a plain dictionary?
interview.answer: An `Item` replicates the standard dictionary API, including its initializer, but limits keys to declared fields. Therefore, assigning or referring to an undefined field raises `KeyError`, helping expose spelling mistakes.
interview.followUp: What alternative item types does Scrapy support? The documentation identifies dictionaries, dataclasses, and attrs objects through itemadapter as well as `Item` objects.

keyPoints: Subclass `scrapy.Item` when modeling structured data emitted by a spider.
Populate and read item values with normal dictionary operations, including constructor arguments.
The declared-field boundary catches accidental references to unknown names.
Attach metadata to fields when downstream processing needs field-specific behavior.
Item compatibility is defined through support by the itemadapter library.
gotchas: Only declared field names are accepted; using an undeclared name raises `KeyError`.

Item pipelines.summary: An item pipeline processes each item yielded by a spider. Components run in order and can change, pass on, or drop an item.
Item pipelines.explanation: After a spider yields an item, Scrapy sends it through the enabled pipeline components in order. Each component can change the item, pass it on by returning it, or stop processing by raising DropItem.

parameters.name: item
parameters.description: The scraped item object passed to the pipeline component.

Item pipelines.returns: process_item must return an item object, or it may raise DropItem.

example.explanation: This pipeline increases prices that exclude VAT. It drops items without a price.

useCases.title: Clean item data
useCases.scenario: Remove unwanted markup or normalize scraped values before output.

useCases.title: Validate items
useCases.scenario: Check required fields and reject incomplete items.

useCases.title: Find duplicates
useCases.scenario: Prevent repeated records from continuing through the pipeline.

useCases.title: Store items
useCases.scenario: Write accepted items to a file or database.

interview.question: What must process_item do?
interview.answer: Scrapy calls process_item for every enabled pipeline component. The method must return an item object for continued processing or raise DropItem to stop processing that item.
interview.followUp: How can a pipeline prepare and release resources? Define open_spider for setup and close_spider for cleanup. Either method may be a coroutine.

interview.question: How do you enable a pipeline?
interview.answer: Set ITEM_PIPELINES to a mapping from the pipeline's import path to an order value. Scrapy runs enabled components sequentially according to the pipeline configuration.
interview.followUp: How would you verify that Scrapy loaded the class? Check the crawl log for the Enabled item pipelines entry.

interview.question: How should a pipeline manage external resources?
interview.answer: A pipeline can use from_crawler to read settings and receive the crawler. For example, a MongoDB pipeline reads its URI and database name, opens the client in open_spider, and closes it in close_spider.
interview.followUp: What should happen if a required resource is unavailable before crawling? open_spider may raise CloseSpider to stop the spider.

keyPoints: An item passes through enabled pipeline components one at a time.
A component can clean, validate, transform, store, or check an item.
The main method receives the scraped item.
process_item, open_spider, and close_spider can be asynchronous.
A pipeline can detect duplicate items and discard them.
A pipeline can save items to a database such as MongoDB.
gotchas: Adding a pipeline class to a spider does not enable it. Add its import path to ITEM_PIPELINES.
If process_item changes an item but returns nothing, the next component receives None.
Raise DropItem only when the item should leave the pipeline.

ITEM_PIPELINES.summary: ITEM_PIPELINES enables Scrapy item pipeline classes and sets their order. Lower order values run first; each pipeline must return the item or raise DropItem.
ITEM_PIPELINES.explanation: Scrapy sends each scraped item through the enabled pipeline classes in order. Each class receives the item in process_item(); it must return the item for continued processing or raise DropItem to stop that item. Add pipeline classes and their order values to ITEM_PIPELINES.

parameters.description: Pipeline class or import path used as a key in ITEM_PIPELINES.

parameters.name: order
parameters.description: Execution order for the pipeline. Lower values run first.

ITEM_PIPELINES.returns: process_item() returns the processed item, or raises DropItem to discard it.

interview.question: How do you enable and order item pipelines?
interview.answer: Scrapy enables pipeline classes through ITEM_PIPELINES. The setting maps each class or import path to an order value, and lower values run first.
interview.followUp: What happens if two entries use the same pipeline class? It is a regular dictionary, so duplicate component definitions should be avoided because the component may be configured more than once.

interview.question: What must process_item() return?
interview.answer: process_item() runs for every pipeline component. It must return an item, or raise DropItem when the item should be removed from later processing.
interview.followUp: Why is returning None a bug? The next pipeline receives None instead of the scraped item, so later processing can fail or produce incorrect output.

interview.question: How does the order value work?
interview.answer: A lower order number runs earlier than a higher one. Scrapy commonly uses numbers from 0 through 1000, but the values themselves are not required to be in that range.
interview.followUp: How can you check that Scrapy loaded a pipeline? Look near the start of the crawl log for the enabled item pipelines message and verify the expected import path appears.

keyPoints: The pipeline receives items after a spider scrapes them.
Pipelines can clean data, validate fields, find duplicates, or store items.
The integer in ITEM_PIPELINES controls when each pipeline class runs.
A class with order 300 runs before one with order 800.
gotchas: Adding a pipeline class to a spider or another location does not enable it. Put its import path in ITEM_PIPELINES.
If process_item() changes an item but returns nothing, the next component receives None.
Do not list the same pipeline twice, including once by class object and once by import path.

ItemLoader.summary: ItemLoader is Scrapy’s convenient, response-aware API for collecting scraped values into items while applying field processors. Add values from selectors or directly, then call load_item() to produce the populated item.
ItemLoader.explanation: ItemLoader is Scrapy’s response-aware extension of itemloaders for collecting scraped values and applying field processors before producing an item. Instantiate it with an existing item or let it create one from default_item_class, add values through extraction or direct methods, and call load_item() when collection is complete.

parameters.name: item
parameters.description: Existing item to populate; when omitted, an item is created using default_item_class.

parameters.name: selector
parameters.description: Selector or response used by extraction methods such as add_xpath() and add_css().

ItemLoader.returns: load_item() returns the populated item after collected values have been processed.

example.title: Populate an item with ItemLoader
example.code:
from scrapy.loader import ItemLoader
from scrapy.item import Item, Field

class Product(Item):
    name = Field()
    price = Field()

loader = ItemLoader(item=Product())
loader.add_value("name", "Widget")
loader.add_value("price", "12.50")
product = loader.load_item()
print(product["name"], product["price"])
example.explanation: Creates a loader for a Product item, collects values, then materializes the populated item with load_item().

useCases.title: Normalize scraped fields
useCases.scenario: A spider extracts product fields from HTML and needs consistent normalization before creating the item.

useCases.title: Combine repeated values
useCases.scenario: A field is assembled from several extracted fragments that must be combined by a processor.

useCases.title: Customize parsing rules
useCases.scenario: Different spiders or source formats require independently configurable field parsing rules.

interview.question: What problem does ItemLoader solve?
interview.answer: ItemLoader provides a structured API for populating scraped items while applying field processors. It accepts an item or can create one automatically, collects values, and returns the populated item through load_item().
interview.followUp: How are multiple values for one field handled? The loader accumulates them and later combines them through the field’s configured processing function.

interview.question: What happens if ItemLoader is created without an item?
interview.answer: You can instantiate it with an item object, or omit the item and rely on the class configured by default_item_class. The latter causes an item object to be created during initialization.
interview.followUp: How would you choose a different item type for a particular loader? Configure or override default_item_class for that loader class or use an explicitly supplied item.

interview.question: When do ItemLoader processors run?
interview.answer: Each item field has an input processor and an output processor. Input processing occurs as values arrive, while output processing is applied when the collected field value is loaded into the final item.
interview.followUp: Why can adding values from different sources remain maintainable? Field-specific processors centralize normalization and combination rules instead of scattering them through spider code.

keyPoints: ItemLoader centralizes the process of filling scraped items instead of requiring direct field assignment.
Scrapy’s class extends the underlying itemloaders functionality with response-oriented integration.
A field may receive several values during collection; the configured processor determines how those values are combined.
Processing is configured independently per field, with separate input and output stages.
Values can be collected from XPath selections, CSS selections, or direct values using the corresponding add methods.

interview.question: What is a link extractor in Scrapy?
interview.answer: Use LinkExtractor, also available as scrapy.linkextractors.LinkExtractor. Call extract_links(response) to get a list of matching Link objects.
interview.followUp: How can a regular Spider use it? Create the extractor as a class attribute or instance member, then call extract_links in a callback and schedule each link URL.

interview.question: How do you filter extracted links?
interview.answer: LxmlLinkExtractor accepts filters such as allow, deny, allow_domains, deny_domains, restrict_xpaths, and restrict_css. Only links that satisfy the configured settings are returned.
interview.followUp: How can extraction be limited by visible link text? Use restrict_text with one regular expression or a list; a list accepts a link when at least one expression matches.

interview.question: What information does a Link contain?
interview.answer: Each result is a Link object. Its fields include the absolute URL, anchor text, URL fragment, and whether the anchor has a nofollow relation.
interview.followUp: What happens to duplicate results? unique=True removes duplicate links; set it to False to keep them.

With unique=True, repeated matching links are removed from the result.
Whitespace is stripped from extracted attributes by default; set strip=False when whitespace is part of the value.

interview.question: What is parse responsible for?
interview.answer: parse is the default callback for responses whose requests do not specify a callback. It receives the Response, extracts data, and can return or yield items and further requests.
interview.followUp: What happens to requests yielded by parse? Scrapy schedules them, downloads their responses, and invokes the callback assigned to each request.

interview.question: What arguments can parse receive?
interview.answer: Its first argument is the Response being processed. It may also receive keyword arguments passed through the request’s cb_kwargs.
interview.followUp: How can a callback remain compatible with arbitrary callback data? Accept keyword parameters, typically through **kwargs, in addition to response.

interview.question: What may parse return?
interview.answer: parse may produce a Request, an item, an iterable containing requests or items, or None. Yielding is commonly used to emit multiple results incrementally.
interview.followUp: Why yield rather than build a list? Yielding lets Scrapy consume results incrementally and avoids requiring all outputs to be held at once.

A spider can omit parse only when every request it sends has its own callback.

interview.question: What is scrapy.Request and how does it fit into crawling?
interview.answer: Request represents an HTTP request that a spider usually creates and the Downloader executes, producing a Response. The callback receives that downloaded response.
interview.followUp: What happens when callback is omitted? Scrapy uses the spider's parse() method.

interview.question: How do callback and errback differ?
interview.answer: The callback handles a successful downloaded response, while errback handles errors raised during processing. The request can also carry headers, cookies, body data, metadata, and an encoding.
interview.followUp: Why use meta? It passes request-scoped data through the crawl, but nested mutable values are not independently copied.

interview.question: Which core arguments control a Request?

interview.followUp: How can request scheduling behavior be adjusted? Use priority and dont_filter, as documented request options.

body carries payload data; string payloads are encoded to bytes.

Request metadata is shallow-copied, so nested objects remain shared.

    status=200,
    headers={"Content-Type": ["application/octet-stream"]},
    body=b"binary data",

)

print(response.url)
print(response.status)
print(response.body)

interview.question: What is scrapy.http.Response used for?
interview.answer: Response represents an HTTP result downloaded by Scrapy and passed to a spider. Its core construction accepts a URL, with status defaulting to 200, plus optional headers, body, and flags.
interview.followUp: How should textual content be handled? Use an encoding-aware subclass such as TextResponse, which provides decoded text access through response.text.

interview.question: What are the important constructor parameters?
interview.answer: The body parameter is bytes, and the base Response is meant for binary payloads. The response URL, status, headers, and flags describe the downloaded result.
interview.followUp: Why not pass decoded text as the body? Because the documented body type is bytes; decoding belongs to an encoding-aware Response subclass.

interview.question: How do headers and flags behave?
interview.answer: Response.headers is a dictionary whose values can be strings for single-valued headers or lists for multi-valued headers. Response.flags receives the initial values for the flags attribute.
interview.followUp: What subclass is appropriate for HTML or other encoded text? TextResponse adds encoding capabilities to the base class.

The downloader normally creates or supplies the response that a spider processes.
url identifies the resource associated with the response.
status records the HTTP result code and defaults to 200 when omitted.
body stores the raw response payload as bytes.
flags can be initialized with labels that annotate the response.

Header values may represent one value or multiple values, so preserve the documented string-or-list shape.

interview.question: What does response.css() return, and how do you select text or attributes?
interview.answer: response.css() returns a SelectorList. Use ::text to select text nodes and ::attr(name) to select an attribute value.
interview.followUp: How do you get every matching value? Call getall() on the SelectorList.

interview.question: What is the difference between get() and getall()?
interview.answer: get() returns the first match, or None when there are no matches. getall() returns a list containing all matches.
interview.followUp: How can you avoid None for a missing value? Pass a default argument, such as get(default="unknown").

interview.question: How can you extract data from elements selected inside another element?
interview.answer: Selectors can be nested because css() and xpath() return selectors. For example, select each image and then read its src attribute with attrib or XPath.
interview.followUp: What does SelectorList.attrib return? It returns the attributes of the first matching element, or an empty dictionary when there are no matches.

keyPoints: A Selector can be built from a TextResponse or from markup supplied as text.
Response objects provide CSS and XPath shortcuts, so callbacks usually do not need to create a Selector manually.
Selection creates selector objects; get() or getall() extracts their string values.
In a CSS query, use ::text to select text nodes below matching elements.
Use ::attr(name) in a CSS query to read an attribute such as href or src.
You can run another CSS or XPath query on each selected element to extract nested data.

get() returns None when there is no match, so use a default value or check the result.
Do not chain ::text or ::attr(...), because the result is already text or an attribute value.

interview.question: What does response.follow do?
interview.answer: response.follow builds and returns a Request using the response as the URL base. The spider must yield that Request so Scrapy can schedule it.
interview.followUp: How would you follow several links? Use response.follow_all with a selector or iterable, then yield from the returned requests.

interview.question: What can be passed to response.follow?
interview.answer: It accepts a relative or absolute URL, a selector that extracts an attribute, or an anchor selector. A callback can be supplied for the resulting request.
interview.followUp: Why is it useful for relative URLs? It resolves them against the current response without a separate urljoin call.

interview.question: When should you use response.follow_all?
interview.answer: response.follow_all creates multiple Request objects. It can receive an iterable of selectors or use a CSS query directly, and the requests must be yielded.
interview.followUp: How can different pages use different callbacks? Pass the required callback when calling response.follow or response.follow_all.

interview.question: What does `response.xpath()` do in Scrapy?
interview.answer: `response.xpath()` evaluates an XPath expression against the current response and returns selector objects. Calling `.get()` returns the first selected value, while the expression can target elements or text nodes.
interview.followUp: Why might XPath be useful instead of CSS? XPath can inspect content, so it can select an element based on text such as a link labeled “Next Page”.

interview.question: What is the difference between `//title` and `//title/text()`?

interview.question: Why use the Scrapy shell?
interview.answer: The Scrapy shell lets you test extraction expressions interactively without running the spider for every change. Start it with `scrapy shell <url>`, then inspect `response` with XPath or CSS.

interview.question: How do you make Scrapy respect robots.txt?

interview.answer: Rule is a CrawlSpider configuration object that associates link extraction with optional callback, processing, error, and follow behavior. CrawlSpider applies the first matching rule when multiple rules match a link.

interview.question: What does link_extractor control?

interview.question: How do you start the Scrapy shell?
interview.answer: Use `scrapy shell <url>` to open the shell with a downloaded page. You can also start it without a URL, and it supports explicit local file paths.
interview.followUp: How do you avoid following a redirect for the initial URL? Use the command option `--no-redirect`; inside the shell, `fetch(url)` follows redirects by default unless passed `redirect=False`.

interview.question: How do you test and extract page data?
interview.answer: The shell provides `response`, which contains the last downloaded page. Use `response.css()` or `response.xpath()` to test selectors, then call methods such as `get()` or `getall()` to extract values.
interview.followUp: What happens after `fetch()`? It downloads the new target and updates related objects, including `response` and `request`.

interview.question: Which built-in objects and shortcuts are available?
interview.answer: The shell creates objects including `crawler`, `spider`, `request`, `response`, and `settings`. Its shortcuts include `shelp()`, `fetch()`, and `view()`.
interview.followUp: How can the shell use a particular spider? Pass `--spider=SPIDER` to bypass automatic spider detection.

Try XPath and CSS selectors interactively while building a spider.

interview.question: What is Selector used for?
interview.answer: Selector is Scrapy’s wrapper for selecting parts of response content. It can be constructed from a TextResponse or from markup passed through text.
interview.followUp: How would you create one without a response? Pass the markup string using Selector(text=...).

interview.question: How do you extract data with Selector?
interview.answer: Use xpath() or css() to locate content, then get() for one result or getall() for all matching results. XPath and CSS selections return selector objects that support further chaining.
interview.followUp: What happens when no result is available from get()? It returns None, while getall() returns an empty list.

interview.question: How is the parsing type determined?
interview.answer: The selector type can be inferred from the response, or forced with type. Supported types include html, xml, and json, with HTML used as the default when text is supplied without an explicit type.
interview.followUp: Why force type? To ensure the supplied content is parsed using the intended rules instead of automatic inference.

process.crawl("quotes")
process.start()

interview.question: What are Scrapy settings and where are project settings normally stored?
interview.answer: Settings are a global key-value mapping used to configure Scrapy components. A project usually places shared values in its settings.py module, and SCRAPY_SETTINGS_MODULE identifies which project settings module is active.
interview.followUp: How do conflicting setting sources resolve? Command-line settings have the highest precedence, followed by spider, project, add-on, command-specific default, and global default settings.

interview.question: How does SCRAPY_SETTINGS_MODULE work?
interview.answer: The environment variable selects the active settings module using Python import syntax, for example myproject.settings. That module must be available on Python's import search path.
interview.followUp: What would you check if selection fails? Verify both the dotted module name and that the project is importable from the current Python path.

interview.question: Which settings source wins when values conflict?
interview.answer: Settings are populated through several mechanisms with defined precedence. Command-line values override spider, project, add-on, command-specific default, and global default values.
interview.followUp: Why does this matter operationally? A command-line override can change runtime behavior without editing the project's settings.py file.

interview.answer: A Spider is a class that defines which requests to send and how to process responses. It normally starts from start_urls, and parse handles each initial response by default.
interview.followUp: How does a callback continue a crawl? It yields Request objects, whose callbacks process later responses.

interview.question: What does Scrapy's xpath() method return?
interview.answer: xpath() evaluates an XPath query against a response or selector and returns matching nodes as a flattened SelectorList. The resulting selectors still support extraction methods such as get() and getall().
interview.followUp: How do you select relative descendants from a nested selector? Use .//, because an XPath beginning with / is absolute to the document.

interview.question: How do you extract values after calling xpath()?
interview.answer: Use get() when one extracted string is needed and getall() when all matching strings are needed. For example, response.xpath("//title/text()").get() returns one title value.
interview.followUp: What happens if no nodes match? The selector list is empty, so get() yields None while getall() yields an empty list.

interview.question: What kinds of data can an XPath expression select?
interview.answer: The argument is an XPath expression, which can select HTML or XML nodes, text nodes, and attributes. For example, //a/@href selects link attributes and //span/text() selects span text.
interview.followUp: How can XML namespace problems be handled? Remove namespaces with Selector.remove_namespaces() before applying the XPath.
